Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events There is no global clock. So how do machines agree on what happened first? AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Leslie Lamport Communications of the ACM 1978 WHAT IT GIVES YOU “Happened-before” and logical clocks, the root of every versioning idea THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Stop trusting wall clocks. Define order by cause and effect, and a simple counter is enough to build a consistent ordering. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS Three friends in three cities are texting about dinner. Each phone’s clock is a little off, so timestamps can lie. But one fact never lies: a reply always comes after the message it answers. Lamport builds a complete theory of order from that single fact. T HE PRO B L E M On one machine, “which came first?” is easy: look at the order of instructions. Across machines it is not. Every server has its own clock, the clocks drift, and a message can take 2 ms or 2 seconds. If server A stamps an event 10:00:00.050 and server B stamps another 10:00:00.040 , you still cannot say B was first. B’s clock may simply run fast. T he qu e st i on Can we define “happened before” without trusting any clock at all? travelled from a to b. Three rules define it: Same machine If a comes before b on one machine, then a → b. Message Sending a message happens before receiving it. Chain If a → b and b → c, then a → c. If neither a → b nor b → a holds, the events are concurrent. That does not mean “at the same moment”. It means no chain of messages connects them, so neither could have influenced the other. H OW I T WORKS The logical clock: a counter that respects cause and effect Keep a counter Every process has one number, starting at 0. Count every event Before each event, add 1 to your counter. Attach it to messages When you send a message, include your current counter. Jump ahead on receive When you receive one, set your counter to max(yours, message) + 1 . P1 P2 P3 P3's "1" and P1's "1" are concurrent max(1, 4) + 1 time → Numbers in circles are clock values. A message forces “send before receive”; events with no message path between them are concurrent. This guarantees one direction: if a → b then clock(a) < clock(b). To get a single order everyone agrees on, break ties with the process ID: compare (clock, processId) . What it is good for Mutual exclusion Everyone broadcasts timestamped requests. The lowest (timestamp, id) goes first. No central lock server. Replicated state machines If every replica applies the same commands in the same order, they stay identical. Paxos and Raft (next chapters) make this fault tolerant. K E Y T E RMS Event Something that happens on one machine: a local step, a send, or a receive. Concurrent Two events with no cause-and-effect path between them. Logical clock A counter that tracks order, not real time. Total order One agreed sequence of all events, with ties broken by process ID. W HA T I T GI V E S UP number cannot tell “earlier” from “unrelated”. Vector clocks fix that (see Dynamo, Chapter 8). Spanner (Chapter 10) goes back to physical clocks, but with an explicit error bar. US E I T I N YOUR WORK version number, a Kafka partition offset, or a hybrid logical clock. In logs and traces, correlate by trace and parent IDs. That is causality, which is what you actually need when debugging. S A Y I T I N A N I NT E RV IE W “Lamport clocks give an ordering that respects causality without synchronized clocks. They cannot detect concurrency; vector clocks can, at the cost of O(number of nodes) metadata.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING Time in a distributed system is a way of ordering events, not a number on a wall.

Paxos Made Simple How can a group of unreliable machines agree on a single value? AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Leslie Lamport ACM SIGACT News 2001 WHAT IT GIVES YOU The majority-quorum logic behind most replicated databases THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Agree on one value by asking a majority twice: first to find out whether a value may already be chosen, then to lock it in. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS Five friends must pick one restaurant by phone, but any of them may lose signal at any time. Before proposing a place, you ask a majority, “has anyone already settled on something?” If yes, you must back that choice, not yours. That one rule is Paxos. T HE PRO B L E M Several machines must agree on one value: who is the leader, or which command is next in the log. Machines crash and restart, and messages arrive late, twice, or never. This is called consensus. Lamport’s assumptions are friendly: nodes may crash and recover but do not lie, and messages may be lost or delayed but not corrupted. T HE BIG IDEA Paxos has three roles. One physical server usually plays all three. Proposer Suggests a value. Several may compete. Acceptor Votes. It is the system’s memory: it remembers what it promised and accepted. Learner Finds out which value was chosen. A value is chosen once a majority of acceptors accepted it. T he on e i ns igh t to r e m e m be r Phase 1 exists to discover whether a value might already be chosen. If it might, the new proposer must adopt it instead of overwriting it. That single rule makes it impossible for two different values to be chosen. H OW I T WORKS The protocol in two phases Single-decree Paxos with 3 acceptors. Any 2 of 3 form a majority, so one crashed acceptor does not stop progress. Prepare A proposer picks a unique, increasing number n and asks a majority of acceptors: “promise to ignore anything numbered below n, and tell me what you already accepted.” Promise Each acceptor promises (if n is its highest so far) and reports the highestnumbered proposal it already accepted, if any. Accept If a majority promised, the proposer sends Accept(n, v) . The value v must be the one from the highest-numbered proposal reported. Only if there was none may it use its own. Accepted An acceptor accepts unless it promised a higher number. When a majority accepts, the value is chosen. Why a majority Cluster size Majority needed Failures tolerated 3 2 1 5 3 2 7 4 3 Any two majorities overlap in at least one node. That overlapping node is the witness that carries knowledge from one round to the next. From one value to a replicated log Real systems need a sequence of decisions, not one. Multi-Paxos runs one Paxos instance per log slot. A stable leader skips Phase 1 for later slots, so the steady-state cost is one round trip: Accept, then Accepted. K E Y T E RMS Consensus Several machines agreeing on one value despite failures. Quorum A group big enough that any two such groups overlap. Usually a majority. Safety Nothing bad ever happens, such as two different values chosen. Liveness Something good eventually happens, such as a value being chosen. W HA T I T GI V E S UP Paxos always guarantees safety, but liveness only with luck: two proposers can keep outbidding each other forever. So you elect a distinguished proposer. The paper leaves leader election, membership changes and many engineering details open. That is why implementations diverge, and why Raft (next chapter) was written. US E I T I N YOUR WORK Paxos-family protocols run underneath Chubby (Ch. 7), Spanner (Ch. 10) and DynamoDB’s per-partition replication (Ch. 11). The practical rule for your own designs: use 2f + 1 replicas to survive f failures, and wait for a majority, never for “all”. S A Y I T I N A N I NT E RV IE W “Paxos chooses a value in two phases. Phase 1 blocks older proposals and discovers any value already accepted; Phase 2 proposes that value. Majority overlap guarantees two different values can never both be chosen.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING Ask a majority twice, and always adopt a value that may already be chosen.

In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft) Consensus that humans can actually understand and implement. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout (Stanford) USENIX Annual Technical Conference 2014 WHAT IT GIVES YOU A readable blueprint for leader election and replicated logs THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Make consensus teachable: one strong leader, randomized election timeouts, and a log that only moves forward. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS A meeting with a chair. Everyone talks to the chair, and the chair announces decisions. If the chair goes quiet, someone clears their throat and calls a vote, and whoever gets a majority becomes the new chair. Raft is that meeting, written as an algorithm. T HE PRO B L E M By 2014 Paxos was the standard answer to consensus, yet students and engineers found it hard, and real systems built from it often looked very different from the paper. Raft’s goal was unusual for a systems paper: design for understandability first, with the same fault tolerance and similar performance. 25.7 vs 20.8 mean quiz score out of 60, Raft vs Paxos (43 students) 33 of 43 students scored higher on Raft 4 message types in Raft 5 servers in a typical cluster, tolerating 2 failures T HE BIG IDEA Raft splits consensus into three smaller problems: leader election, log replication and safety. At any moment one server is the leader. Clients talk to it, and log entries flow one way only: leader → followers. H OW I T WORKS Three states, and elections sees a higher term sees a leader or higher term Every Raft server is always in exactly one of three states. Wait for heartbeats A follower expects regular messages from the leader. Time out If none arrive within its election timeout, it becomes a candidate, adds 1 to the term number, and asks for votes. Win a majority A majority of votes makes it the leader. Each server votes once per term. Lead The new leader sends heartbeats immediately so nobody else starts an election. T he tr ick t h a t a vo id s e n dle ss sp li t vot e s Each server picks a random timeout from a range (the paper suggests 150–300 ms). Usually exactly one server wakes first, wins, and sends heartbeats before anyone else wakes up. Why randomness matters (measured on 5 servers) No randomness usually over 10 s 5 ms of randomness 287 ms median 50 ms of randomness 513 ms worst case Each bar shows the statistic the authors reported for that setting. Replicating the log The leader appends the client’s command to its log and sends AppendEntries to followers. This same message doubles as the heartbeat. Each message names the entry just before the new ones. A follower that lacks it refuses, and the leader walks backwards until the logs match, then overwrites any conflicting tail. #1 #2 #3 #4 #5 #6 Leader term 1 term 1 term 1 term 2 term 3 term 3 Follower 1 term 1 term 1 term 1 term 2 term 3 term 3 Follower 2 term 1 term 1 term 1 term 2 term 3 Follower 3 term 1 term 1 term 1 term 2 Follower 4 term 1 term 1 term 1 c omm i tt ed up to #5 #6: on 2 of 5 not yet Entry #5 is on 3 of 5 servers (a majority), so it is safe. Entry #6 is on only 2, so it is not committed yet. An entry is committed once it is stored on a majority. Only then is it applied to the state machine. Safety: the two rules people forget Election restriction A server votes only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own (last term first, then length). So a new leader always holds every committed entry. Commit rule A leader never commits entries from earlier terms by counting replicas. It commits one entry from its own term, and that commits everything before it. Membership changes and snapshots To add or remove servers, Raft uses joint consensus: during the change, decisions need majorities of both the old and new configurations, so two independent leaders can never exist. Long logs are trimmed with snapshots. K E Y T E RMS Term A numbered period with at most one leader. It acts as a logical clock. AppendEntries The leader’s message that carries new log entries and also acts as a heartbeat. Committed Stored on a majority, so it can never be lost. State machine The service that applies committed commands in order. W HA T I T GI V E S UP All writes go through one leader, so write throughput is limited by it. Scaling means many Raft groups (sharding), which is what Spanner and DynamoDB do with Paxos groups. Outside the paper: etcd and Consul are built on Raft, and Kafka’s KRaft mode uses a Raft-based quorum for metadata in place of ZooKeeper. US E I T I N YOUR WORK When you design a replicated component, define states, terms (epochs) and one writer. An epoch number that fences old leaders is the same idea as a fencing token for distributed locks (Chapter 7). “Raft elects a leader with randomized timeouts, replicates a log with AppendEntries, commits on majority, and uses an election restriction so a new leader always holds all committed entries.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING One leader, one direction of flow , and a vote that only goes to an up-to-date log.

The Google File System A file system built on the assumption that machines are always breaking. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff, Shun-Tak Leung SOSP 2003 · Google WHAT IT GIVES YOU Control/data plane separation and designing for failure THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Store giant files on cheap machines by keeping metadata in one inmemory master and moving the data directly between clients and replicas. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS A library with one librarian and many shelves. The librarian never carries books; they only keep the catalogue, in their head, of which shelf holds what. You ask the librarian where a book is, then walk to the shelf yourself. GFS works the same way. T HE PRO B L E M Google needed storage for crawling and indexing the web: files of many gigabytes, thousands of cheap machines, and a workload that mostly appends and reads sequentially. The authors built around four observations: Failures are normal on commodity hardware, not exceptional. Files are huge (multi-GB), so small-file tricks matter little. Mostly append and sequential read. Random overwrites are rare. Co-design file system and applications, so the API can be relaxed (for example, an atomic record-append). Files are cut into fixed 64 MB chunks. Each chunk has an immutable 64-bit ID, is stored as a plain Linux file on a chunkserver, and is copied to three machines by default (spread over racks). One master keeps all metadata in memory: the file names, the file-to-chunk mapping, and where each chunk lives. Clients ask the master only where, then read and write the data directly with chunkservers. The bytes never pass through the master. H OW I T WORKS Control (orange, dashed) goes through the master. Data (slate) goes straight between client and chunkservers. A write, step by step Ask the master The client asks which chunkserver holds the lease (the primary) for the chunk. Master replies It returns the primary and the replicas. The client caches this. Push the data The client sends the data to the nearest replica, which forwards it down a chain. Write request The client then tells the primary to perform the write. Primary orders it The primary gives the write a serial number and tells the secondaries to apply it. Acknowledge Secondaries confirm to the primary, and the primary confirms to the client. Why one master is enough (the metadata math) The master stores under 64 bytes of metadata per 64 MB chunk. As a back-ofenvelope, 1 PB is about 16.8 million chunks, so roughly 1 GB of RAM per petabyte. It does not even persist chunk locations: it simply asks chunkservers through heartbeats. Changes go to a replicated operation log, plus checkpoints. Read-only shadow masters serve reads if the master is down. 64 MB chunk size (huge on purpose) 3 replicas per chunk by default 60 s initial lease to a primary < 64 B master metadata per chunk Relaxed consistency, on purpose Record append lets many clients append to the same file at once. GFS chooses the offset and guarantees the record lands at least once. Duplicates and padding are possible, so applications write self-validating records with checksums or unique IDs. Running a cluster that always has failures Re-replication: in one failure test, about 15,000 chunks (600 GB) were restored in 23.2 minutes. Garbage collection: deleted files are renamed, then reclaimed lazily (hidden files are removed after three days by default). Integrity: chunkservers checksum every 64 KB block and verify on read. Real cluster in the paper Cluster A Cluster B Chunkservers 342 227 Disk (used / available) 55 TB / 72 TB 155 TB / 180 TB Files 735 thousand 737 thousand Metadata at master 48 MB 60 MB K E Y T E RMS Chunk A fixed 64 MB piece of a file. Lease Temporary permission for one replica (the primary) to order writes for a chunk. Control plane / data Deciding where things go, versus actually moving the plane bytes. W HA T I T GI V E S UP The single master is a bottleneck and a single point of failure by design. It works for big files and modest metadata; Google later moved to a successor system as scale grew. Large chunks hurt small files: one hot small file lives on one chunk, so a few servers get hammered. US E I T I N YOUR WORK Separate the control plane from the data plane. A metadata service decides; storage nodes move bytes. The same split shows up in HDFS (NameNode and DataNodes) and in object-store designs where your service hands out pre-signed URLs and never proxies large files. S A Y I T I N A N I NT E RV IE W “GFS keeps all metadata in one master’s memory and lets clients stream data directly to chunkservers. 64 MB chunks keep metadata tiny, and leases give a single primary per chunk to order writes.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING A small brain that only points , and many workers that move the bytes.

MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters Write two functions. Let the framework deal with ten thousand cores. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Jeffrey Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat OSDI 2004 · Google WHAT IT GIVES YOU The mental model behind batch and stream processing THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Express a huge computation as map then reduce, and let the runtime handle partitioning, scheduling and failures by simply re-running tasks. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS Counting votes in a huge election. Hundreds of clerks each count one box and write tallies per candidate (map). Then all tallies for the same candidate go to one person who adds them up (reduce). If a clerk falls ill, someone else just recounts that box. T HE PRO B L E M Google engineers wrote many small programs to process huge data: crawled pages, logs, inverted indexes. The computation was simple; the plumbing was not. Splitting data, spreading work over thousands of machines, surviving failures, moving data between stages. The authors extracted that plumbing into a library. T HE BIG IDEA You write two functions. The framework does everything else. map(key, value) Reads one piece of input and emits intermediate (key, value) pairs. reduce(key, [values]) Combines all values that share one key into a result. H OW I T WORKS Input splits Map Shuffle & sort Reduce Output word count: map(line) → (word, 1) reduce(word, [1,1,…]) → (word, total) Word count, the classic example. Everything between map and reduce is done by the framework. Think of it in Java terms Map counts = lines.stream() .flatMap(l -> Arrays.stream(l.split(" "))) // map .collect(groupingBy(w -> w, counting())); // shuffle + reduce Same shape, except MapReduce runs it over terabytes on thousands of machines. How a job runs Split the input The input is cut into splits (the paper mentions 16–64 MB). A master hands splits to idle workers, preferring one that already holds the data on its local disk. Map Map workers write results to local disk, partitioned into R buckets with hash(key) mod R . Shuffle and reduce Reduce workers fetch their bucket from every map worker, sort by key, and call reduce. Write the output Reduce outputs go to the distributed file system (GFS, Chapter 4). Fault tolerance: just run it again Worker dies: the master notices missed pings and re-runs its tasks. Even finished map tasks are re-run, because their output sat on the dead machine’s local disk. Safe re-execution: deterministic functions plus an atomic rename of output mean duplicates do no harm. Stragglers: near the end of a job, the master launches backup copies of the slowest tasks. Whichever finishes first wins. Bad records: the framework can skip input records that repeatedly crash the user code. Master failure: the simple answer is to abort and re-run the job. Smart optimisations Combiner A mini-reduce on the map side (for example, pre-summing word counts) to shrink the shuffle. Locality Move computation to the data, not data to the computation. Network bandwidth was the scarce resource. Partition function Controls which reducer gets which key. Skewed keys mean one slow reducer. Ordering Within a partition, keys are processed in sorted order. NUM BE RS WORT H KNOW I N G Sorting 1 TB: why backup tasks and re-execution matter Normal run 891 s No backup tasks 1,283 s (+44%) 200 workers killed 933 s (+5%) From the paper’s sort benchmark on a cluster of roughly 1,800 machines. 891 s to sort 1 TB in the paper’s cluster +44% slower without backup tasks +5% slower after killing 200 workers mid-run 1,000+ jobs per day at Google when written K E Y T E RMS Shuffle Moving map output so all values with the same key meet at one reducer. Straggler A task that runs much slower than its peers and delays the whole job. Idempotent Safe to run twice: the result is the same as running once. W HA T I T GI V E S UP Every stage writes to disk and the shuffle is all-to-all, so chained or iterative jobs are slow. That gap led to in-memory engines like Spark. One hot key sends all its values to one reducer. US E I T I N YOUR WORK Build batch jobs from idempotent, deterministic tasks so any task can be retried safely. That is the design rule behind retries in Kafka consumers, Spring Batch restarts and your own backfills. S A Y I T I N A N I NT E RV IE W “MapReduce hides distribution behind map and reduce. Fault tolerance comes from deterministic tasks that can be re-executed, and backup tasks fix stragglers.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING If a task can be safely repeated, failure stops being scary.

Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data A sorted map that spans thousands of machines. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Fay Chang, Jeffrey Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, et al. OSDI 2006 · Google WHAT IT GIVES YOU LSM trees, row-key design, and wide-column modelling THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Store petabytes by sharding a sorted (row, column, time) map into tablets that live on GFS and are coordinated by Chubby. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS A giant dictionary printed in order, torn into volumes. Each volume (tablet) sits on a different shelf, and a small index tells you which volume holds your word. New entries go in a notepad first and get merged into fresh printed volumes later. T HE PRO B L E M Google products such as web indexing, Earth and finance needed to store structured data at petabyte scale, from batch jobs to latency-sensitive serving. A file system (GFS) was too low-level, and a relational database could not spread across thousands of machines. Bigtable is the middle path. T HE BIG IDEA The paper calls it a sparse, distributed, persistent, multi-dimensional sorted map. Plainly: look up by (row key, column, timestamp) and get bytes back. column "contents:" column family "anchor:" com.cnn.www row key (reversed domain) t6 <html>… v3 t5 <html>… v2 t3 <html>… v1 cnnsi.com → "CNN" my.look.ca → "CNN.com" rows are sorted by key; a range of rows = a tablet The paper’s “webtable” example. Rows are sorted by key and split into tablets. Rows are sorted by key. A contiguous range of rows is a tablet, the unit of distribution and load balancing. Column families are declared up front. Columns inside a family are created freely. Timestamps keep several versions of a cell. Only single-row transactions. No atomicity across rows. H OW I T WORKS Standing on other building blocks GFS (Ch. 4) Stores the commit log and the SSTable files. Bigtable does not do its own replication. Chubby (Ch. 7) Picks the single active master, tracks live tablet servers, and stores the root of the location hierarchy and schema. SSTable An immutable, sorted key→value file with a block index. Immutable means no locks on reads. Tablet server Serves reads and writes for a set of tablets. Clients talk to it directly. Life of a write and a read Writes are cheap sequential appends. Reads pay for it by merging a few places. Write Append to the commit log in GFS, then insert into the in-memory memtable. Flush When the memtable is full, write it out as a new SSTable (a “minor compaction”). Later, merge SSTables (“major compaction”) to keep reads fast. Read Merge a view of the memtable and all relevant SSTables. The newest data wins. How a client finds the right tablet Chubby file Holds the location of the root tablet. Root tablet Points to the METADATA tablets. METADATA tablets Say which server holds each user tablet. User tablet Your data, as SSTables in GFS. Three hops, and clients cache locations aggressively. With an empty cache a lookup costs three round trips; with a stale cache, up to six. Most lookups never touch the hierarchy. Performance refinements Locality groups keep column families that are read together in the same files. Compression works very well because similar pages sit next to each other. Bloom filters avoid touching files that cannot contain a row, and several cache layers reduce disk reads. NUM BE RS WORT H KNOW I N G 3 levels in the tablet location hierarchy 100–200 MB default tablet size 2³⁴ tablets addressable with 128 MB METADATA tablets 1 row the largest unit of atomic transaction K E Y T E RMS Tablet A contiguous range of rows, served by one tablet server. SSTable An immutable, sorted file of key→value pairs. Memtable The in-memory sorted buffer where new writes land first. Compaction Merging immutable files in the background. W HA T I T GI V E S UP No joins, no secondary indexes, no multi-row transactions. A hot row key, or a key that only ever increases, piles every write onto one tablet. Your row-key design is your schema, your index and your load balancer all at once. US E I T I N YOUR WORK or bucket prefix to timestamp-like keys. The log + memtable + SSTable (LSM tree) pattern here also powers Cassandra (Ch. 9). HBase is the open-source implementation of this very paper. “Bigtable is a sorted, versioned map sharded into tablets. Writes go to a commit log and memtable, flush to immutable SSTables on GFS, and Chubby coordinates the master and location root.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING Writes are appends; sorted immutable files make reads and scans cheap.

The Chubby Lock Service for Loosely- Coupled Distributed Systems One reliable place for the whole company to agree on “who is in charge?” AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Mike Burrows OSDI 2006 · Google WHAT IT GIVES YOU Leader election, leases and fencing tokens. The ancestor of ZooKeeperstyle services THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Instead of giving everyone a consensus library, give them a Paxosbacked lock service with a file API, and let coarse locks do the coordination. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS A single sign-in sheet at the front desk of a huge company. Whoever signs on the “team lead” line is the lead, and everyone can read the sheet. Nobody has to run their own election. Chubby is that sheet, kept safe by five copies. T HE PRO B L E M Every distributed service at Google needed a way to elect a master or agree on small pieces of configuration, and teams were tempted to write their own consensus code (usually badly). Burrows’ answer: build one shared, highly available lock service that everyone calls, like a very small, very reliable file system. Why a lock service, not a consensus library? Developers already understand locks and files, so existing programs need few changes. A service that starts single-server can later be replicated without rewriting the client. Small files also let you announce results (who is the master?), not only agree on them. T HE BIG IDEA /ls/cell/bigtable/master-lock ← whoever holds this lock is the master A tiny, highly available, replicated file system used mostly as a lock and naming service. A cell of 5 replicas elects a master using Paxos. The master holds a lease of a few seconds. Three replicas must be up for the cell to work. A file-like API: whole-file reads and writes of small files, advisory read/write locks, and event notifications. Coarse-grained locks: held for hours or days, not milliseconds. So the service sees little traffic and can tolerate short outages. Sessions and KeepAlive: a client’s session is extended by periodic KeepAlive calls (default 12 s). If the master fails over, a 45 s grace period lets sessions survive. Consistent caching: clients cache files, and the master invalidates caches on a write instead of relying on timeouts. Locks are not safe on their own: sequencers A client holding a lock can pause (garbage collection, network trouble) and wake up after the lock expired and went to someone else. Chubby’s answer is the sequencer: a token describing the lock and its generation. The protected server checks it and rejects stale holders. Today we call this a fencing token. UPDATE job SET owner = :me, token = :t WHERE id = :id AND token What Chubby servers spend time on (ten-minute snapshot) KeepAlive 93% GetStat 2% Open 1% CreateSession 1% GetContents 0.4% 93% of requests were just clients saying “I’m still alive”. Lock acquisitions were a tiny fraction. What operating it taught them People misuse shared services. One team rewrote a 1.5 MB file on every user action, which led to the 256 kB file limit and quotas. Outages were mostly short: over about 700 cell-days there were 61 outages. Most lasted 15 seconds or less, and 52 were under 30 s. Keep it cheap: KeepAlives dominate traffic, so clients and proxies can multiplex them. NUM BE RS WORT H KNOW I N G 5 replicas per cell 12 s default session lease 45 s grace period across master fail-over 90,000 clients one master has served directly K E Y T E RMS Lease A permission that expires unless renewed. Session A client’s ongoing relationship with the cell, kept alive by KeepAlive. Advisory lock A lock that is only respected by programs that choose to check it. Fencing token A number that only grows. Servers reject requests with an older number. W HA T I T GI V E S UP It is a central service. Its failure affects many systems at once, so it is run conservatively. Locks are advisory, not enforced, and clients must handle “jeopardy” and expired sessions. US E I T I N YOUR WORK Use fencing in your own code. With any lock (Redis, ZooKeeper, a database row), carry a monotonically increasing token and reject writes with an older one. Never assume that holding a lock means you still hold it when you write. S A Y I T I N A N I NT E RV IE W “Chubby is a Paxos-replicated lock and small-file service. Coarse-grained locks, sessions and sequencers give leader election and naming without every team building consensus.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING A lock is only safe if the resource it protects can reject a stale holder.

Dynamo : Amazon’s Highly Available Key-value Store The shopping cart that must always accept an item. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Giuseppe DeCandia, Deniz Hastorun, et al. (Amazon) SOSP 2007 · Amazon WHAT IT GIVES YOU Tunable consistency and the “always writable” philosophy THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Choose availability over strong consistency: replicate on a ring, accept writes anywhere, keep versions with vector clocks, and merge later. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS Two people add items to the same shared shopping list on separate phones, with no signal. Both lists are valid. Dynamo’s answer: do not block either person. When they reconnect, keep both versions and merge them, so nothing is lost. T HE PRO B L E M On Amazon’s e-commerce platform, an unavailable shopping cart means lost orders. Service-level agreements were written at the 99.9th percentile, not the average. The paper cites a typical SLA of 300 ms for 99.9% of requests at a peak of 500 requests per second. Amazon’s engineers concluded that for many services, availability matters more than strict consistency. So Dynamo is always writable: it accepts writes even during failures and resolves conflicts later. Problem Technique Benefit Partitioning Consistent hashing + virtual nodes Incremental scaling; even load Writes during Sloppy quorum + hinted Always writable failures handoff Conflicting Vector clocks, reconciled on No lost updates; app decides the versions read merge Permanent failures Merkle-tree anti-entropy Replicas repair themselves cheaply Membership Gossip No central registry or master T HE BIG IDEA Keys and nodes are hashed onto a ring. The first node clockwise from the key is its coordinator, and the key is also stored on the next N − 1 nodes. Every node can coordinate; there is no leader. N = 3 copies of every key W = 2 replicas must acknowledge a write R = 2 replicas must answer a read R + W > N → read and write sets overlap so a read normally sees the latest write Three copies (N = 3). A write needs 2 acks (W = 2); a read asks 2 replicas (R = 2). Each physical node owns many small ring positions (virtual nodes), so load is even, stronger machines can take more, and a failed node’s work spreads over many peers. H OW I T WORKS Quorums you can tune A write succeeds after W replicas acknowledge. A read asks R replicas. With R + W > N the sets overlap, so a read normally sees the latest write. The paper’s common setting is (N, R, W) = (3, 2, 2) . Lower W for faster writes, lower R for faster reads, and accept some staleness. S l oppy quorum If one of the N home nodes is down, Dynamo writes to the next healthy node on the ring with a hint saying whose data it is. When the owner returns, the hint is handed back. You stay available, but you give up the strict overlap guarantee. Versioning with vector clocks Two clients update the cart at the same time while the network is split. Each version carries a vector clock: a list of (node, counter) pairs. If one clock covers another, the older version is dropped. If neither does, they are siblings and both are returned to the client to merge. In production, 99.94% of requests saw exactly one version. Healing: gossip and Merkle trees Nodes gossip membership and failure information with random peers. Replicas compare Merkle trees (hash trees) of their key ranges, so they find differing data by exchanging a few hashes, not whole datasets. NUM BE RS WORT H KNOW I N G 300 ms typical SLA at the 99.9th percentile 3·2·2 common N, R, W settings 99.94% of requests saw a single version 0 hops most requests routed directly to the right node K E Y T E RMS Consistent hashing Placing keys and nodes on a ring so adding a node moves only a small share of keys. Vector clock Per-node counters that tell “newer” from “conflicting”. Hinted handoff A stand-in node holds a write until the real owner returns. Anti-entropy Background comparison and repair of replicas. W HA T I T GI V E S UP Conflict resolution leaks into application code, and a classic anomaly is that a removed cart item can reappear. Every node keeping routing information about all others limits how far the design scales. Dynamo was an internal system, not a product. DynamoDB (Chapter 11) is a very different design: a leader-based Paxos group per partition. US E I T I N YOUR WORK Treat (replicas, write quorum, read quorum) as per-use-case knobs, make writes idempotent, and decide up front how conflicts merge: last-write-wins, union, or CRDT-style. Read repair and hinted handoff reappear in Cassandra (Chapter 9). S A Y I T I N A N I NT E RV IE W “Dynamo trades consistency for availability: consistent hashing with virtual nodes, N/R/W quorums, sloppy quorum with hinted handoff, vector clocks, and Merkle-tree anti-entropy. It never blocks writes.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING Never refuse a write; keep every version and merge when you can.

Cassandra: A Decentralized Structured Storage System Take Dynamo’s distribution, add Bigtable’s storage engine. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Avinash Lakshman, Prashant Malik (Facebook) LADIS workshop; later ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 2009–2010 · Facebook WHAT IT GIVES YOU Wide-column modelling and the LSM write path THE PAPER IN ONE LINE A leaderless, always-on database that distributes like Dynamo and stores like Bigtable, built to power Inbox Search. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS Take the delivery network of one company (any branch can take an order, no head office) and the warehouse of another (everything is logged first, then filed in sorted crates). Cassandra is the two combined. T HE PRO B L E M Facebook’s Inbox Search had to index messages for hundreds of millions of users: billions of writes per day, growth by adding commodity machines, and no single point of failure. The Cassandra paper describes a system for it, built from the best parts of two famous designs. Dynamo (Amazon) ring · replication gossip · no master tunable consistency Bigtable (Google) commit log · memtable SSTable · compaction = Cassandra Cassandra took its distribution model from Dynamo and its storage model from Bigtable. T HE BIG IDEA Distribution: the Dynamo half Partitioning: consistent hashing on a ring with an order-preserving hash. A key’s coordinator is the next node clockwise. Instead of virtual nodes, lightly loaded nodes move on the ring to relieve busy ones. Replication: each item lives on N nodes. Strategies: rack-unaware, rack-aware, and datacenter-aware (survive a whole data centre). Membership: a gossip protocol, so every node learns about the others with no central registry. Failure detection: the φ accrual detector outputs a suspicion level from observed heartbeat timing, instead of a hard yes or no. Detecting a dead node in a 100-node cluster Older detector about 2 minutes φ accrual (φ = 5) about 15 seconds The detector adapts to network jitter instead of using a fixed timeout. Storage: the Bigtable half The log-structured write path: writes are sequential appends, so they are fast. Reads pay for it. Commit log on a dedicated disk (sequential appends) gives durability. It is rolled at 128 MB. Memtable is updated only after the log write succeeds, then flushed to an immutable SSTable when it crosses a size threshold. SSTables carry a block index and an in-memory Bloom filter, so most reads touch very few files. Compaction merges SSTables in the background. It is disk-heavy, but keeps reads fast. The data model A table is a distributed multidimensional map indexed by a row key (typically 16–36 bytes). Operations on a single row key are atomic per replica. Columns live in column families, either simple or super (a column family inside a column family). Inbox Search used super columns: for term search a word maps to message IDs; for interaction search a recipient maps to message IDs. NUM BE RS WORT H KNOW I N G 150 nodes in the production cluster, across two coasts 50+ TB of user data on that cluster 7 TB of inbox data indexed from MySQL for 100M+ users ≈ 15 s to detect a failed node at φ = 5 (vs ≈ 2 min) Read latency (ms) Interaction search Term search Minimum 7.69 7.78 Median 15.69 18.27 Maximum 26.13 44.41 T he n vs . now The paper dates from Facebook’s time with the system. Today’s Apache Cassandra has evolved: it no longer relies on ZooKeeper for range assignment, and its default partitioner hashes keys rather than preserving order. Treat the paper as the origin story and the docs as the current truth. K E Y T E RMS Wide-column Rows that can hold very many columns, grouped in families. Gossip Nodes sharing news with random peers until everyone knows. φ accrual detector A failure detector that reports how suspicious a silent node is, not just alive or dead. W HA T I T GI V E S UP No joins, and queries must be planned before the schema. Heavy compaction competes with reads for disk. With no leader, conflicting writes are resolved by simple rules (such as last-writewins) instead of by transactions. US E I T I N YOUR WORK Model tables around queries, not entities. Pick the partition key so one query hits one partition, avoid unbounded partitions, and denormalise on purpose. The write path (log → memtable → SSTable) is why writes are cheap and reads are the expensive side. S A Y I T I N A N I NT E RV IE W “Cassandra is Dynamo’s ring, gossip and replication on top of Bigtable’s commitlog, memtable and SSTable storage engine, built for Inbox Search. Writes are fast; you design the model around your queries.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING Design the table for the query you will run, not for the data you have.

Spanner : Google’s Globally-Distributed Database Global transactions, made possible by a clock that admits its own error. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR James C. Corbett, Jeffrey Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, et al. (27 authors) OSDI 2012 · Google WHAT IT GIVES YOU External consistency, TrueTime, and the price of global strong consistency THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Combine Paxos-replicated shards, two-phase commit and GPS/atomicclock timestamps with bounded error to get globally consistent transactions. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS Two judges in different countries stamp rulings. Their watches may differ by a few milliseconds, so each judge says: “it is somewhere between 10:00:00.001 and 10:00:00.007”, and waits out the uncertainty before announcing. Now any later ruling, anywhere, is guaranteed a later stamp. T HE PRO B L E M Bigtable gave scale but only single-row transactions. Google’s ads database (F1) needed real transactions across rows and data centres, SQL-like queries, and replicas spread around the world. Spanner is the first system the paper claims distributes data at global scale and still supports externally consistent distributed transactions. E xt e rn a l c ons i st e n c y i n on e s e nt e n ce If transaction T1 finishes before T2 starts in real time, then T1’s commit timestamp is smaller than T2’s. Everyone, anywhere, sees them in that order. T HE BIG IDEA Zone 1 (a data centre) Zone 2 (a data centre) Zone 3 (a data centre) Paxos group 1 ★ Paxos group 1 Paxos group 1 Paxos group 2 Paxos group 2 ★ Paxos group 2 Paxos group 3 Paxos group 3 Paxos group 3 ★ ★ = leader · each group keeps one replica in every zone a transaction across groups: leaders run two-phase commit, and every step is made durable by Paxos Spanner = many Paxos groups (for replication) + two-phase commit across groups (for transactions). Data is sharded into tablets; each tablet has a Paxos group with replicas in different zones. Leaders hold leases (10 s by default). A directory is a set of contiguous keys sharing a prefix, the smallest unit of placement. The paper estimates a 50 MB directory moves in a few seconds. A spanserver handles 100–1,000 tablets. Zones have from a hundred to several thousand spanservers. Data is semi-relational: schematised tables, SQL-like queries, and versioned values stamped with commit time. H OW I T WORKS TrueTime: admitting that clocks are uncertain Instead of returning one time, TrueTime returns an interval [earliest, latest] that is guaranteed to contain the true time. It relies on GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every data centre. The uncertainty ε is typically a sawtooth of about 1–7 ms, around 4 ms most of the time, and generally under 10 ms. ε (uncertainty) is about 1–7 ms pick commit TT.after(s) is true: s is surely in the past release locks, reply timestamp s = latest TT . now () = [ e a r lie st , l a t e st ] earliest latest TrueTime does not say what time it is; it says the time is somewhere inside a small interval. Pick a timestamp The leader picks a commit timestamp s equal to the latest edge of the interval. Wait It waits until TT.after(s) is true. The expected wait is at least 2ε. Release Now s is definitely in the past everywhere, so any transaction that starts later gets a larger timestamp. Locks are released and the client is told. T he w h o le tr ick Pay a few milliseconds of waiting, and get externally consistent, global transactions. Two-phase commit: mean latency (ms) by number of participants 1 participant 17 10 participants 30 50 participants 42.7 100 participants 71.4 200 participants 150.5 From Spanner’s microbenchmarks: latency stays modest up to about 50 participants, then climbs. ≈ 14 ms write latency in the 3-replica test ≈ 1.3 ms read-only transaction latency ≈ 10 s throughput recovery after a leader is hardkilled 72 / 103 ms mean single-site / multi-site commit latency in F1 In the F1 case study, replicas sat in five locations (two on the US west coast, three on the east). A schema change could run without blocking, by picking a future timestamp for the change: timestamps solving a problem that normally needs a lock. K E Y T E RMS External consistency Transaction order matches real-time order, everywhere. Two-phase commit A protocol where a coordinator asks all participants to (2PC) prepare, then tells them all to commit. TrueTime A clock API that returns a time interval with guaranteed bounds. Commit wait Deliberate pause so a timestamp is safely in the past. W HA T I T GI V E S UP Needs special clock hardware and operations expertise. Every write pays the commit wait plus Paxos round trips; multi-region writes cost tens of milliseconds. Pessimistic locking means contended rows hurt. US E I T I N YOUR WORK When you need strong consistency, you pay in latency, so offer clients a choice: strong reads versus bounded-staleness reads. The same trade-off shows up in Cloud Spanner, DynamoDB’s strongly versus eventually consistent reads, and Cassandra’s consistency levels. S A Y I T I N A N I NT E RV IE W “Spanner shards data into Paxos groups, uses two-phase commit across groups, and TrueTime’s bounded clock error plus commit wait to assign timestamps that respect real-time order, giving external consistency.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING Do not pretend you know the time. Bound the error, then wait it out.

Amazon DynamoDB: A Scalable, Predictably Performant, and Fully Managed NoSQL Database Service Fifteen years after Dynamo: the lessons from running it as a cloud service. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Mostafa Elhemali, Niall Gallagher, Nicholas Gordon, et al. (AWS) USENIX Annual Technical Conference 2022 · Amazon WHAT IT GIVES YOU Admission control, multi-tenancy, and managed-service engineering THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Run a NoSQL database for everyone by pairing leader-based Paxos replication with admission control that keeps latency predictable. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS A shared swimming pool with lane tickets. Each swimmer gets a fixed number of tickets per second. A heavy swimmer cannot take over the pool and slow everyone else down. That ticket system is what makes the pool’s speed predictable. T HE PRO B L E M DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL service. The paper’s thesis: customers care less about peak speed than about predictable performance, the same single-digitmillisecond latency for the first request and the billionth, regardless of table size or what the neighbours are doing. N ot t he 2007 D yn a mo Despite the name, DynamoDB is not Dynamo (Chapter 8) running as a service. Its replication is leader-based, not leaderless. 89.2M requests per second at peak, Prime Day 2021 99.999% availability SLA for global tables 2 of 3 replicas needed to acknowledge a write 35 days point-in-time restore window T HE BIG IDEA route → check capacity → leader replicates across zones Life of a write: route, check capacity, then leader-based replication across Availability Zones. A table is split into partitions, each owning a contiguous key range, replicated across three Availability Zones. Replicas form a group using Multi-Paxos. The leader holds a renewable lease and serves writes and strongly consistent reads. Log replicas store only recent write-ahead-log entries, no data. They take part as acceptors and make healing cheaper. Request routers authenticate, authorize and route each call using a metadata service. An auto-admin service watches fleet health, replaces bad replicas and splits partitions. Predictability: from provisioned capacity to global admission control Customers buy read capacity units (one strongly consistent read per second, up to 4 KB) and write capacity units (one write per second, up to 1 KB). Enforcing that fairly across a shared fleet took several generations: Token bucket tokens left: 7 of 10 refills at the provisioned rate (e.g. 100 write units / s) unused tokens are kept up to 300 s, so short bursts are absorbed Admission control with token buckets, the mechanism behind “predictable performance”. Partition-level limits Each partition got a share of the table’s capacity. Problem: a hot partition was throttled even though the table had spare capacity. Bursting A partition can use unused capacity, retained for up to 300 seconds, to absorb spikes. Adaptive capacity Boosted skewed partitions. The paper says it removed over 99.99% of throttling from skewed access. Global admission control Request routers hold token buckets for the table and refill them from a central service every few seconds. Partition-level throttling stays as a safety net. Operational lessons the paper shares Metadata caches hide a failure mode. When routers’ caches were cold, metadata traffic could spike to about 75% and overload the service. They replaced the caches with an in-memory distributed store (MemDS), so lookups stay fast and traffic stays steady. The original cache hit rate was about 99.75%. Backups never touch live traffic. Full backups are built from archived write-ahead logs in S3. On-demand mode can instantly serve up to double a table’s previous peak. Transactions: multi-item ACID transactions were added without hurting scalability or availability. Dynamo (2007) vs DynamoDB (2022) Dynamo (2007) DynamoDB (2022) Replication Leaderless, sloppy quorum Leader per partition, Multi-Paxos Consistency Eventual; app reconciles siblings Eventual or strong reads; one leader orders writes Delivered as Internal service Multi-tenant managed service with SLAs Biggest Availability during failures Predictable performance for everyone challenge K E Y T E RMS Admission control capacity. Deciding whether to accept a request, based on available Token bucket A counter that refills at a fixed rate; each request spends a token. Availability Zone (AZ) An isolated data centre inside a region. Hot partition One key range receiving far more traffic than the others. W HA T I T GI V E S UP The model is limited: you design access patterns around your keys. A hot key still hits one partition’s limits. Cost scales with provisioned throughput or on-demand usage. US E I T I N YOUR WORK Your own APIs need admission control too. A token bucket per tenant (see Spring Cloud Gateway or Bucket4j) stops noisy neighbours. And watch for modal behaviour: a design that is fast only when a cache is warm will fall over exactly when you restart. S A Y I T I N A N I NT E RV IE W “DynamoDB gives predictable single-digit-ms performance through partitioned Multi-Paxos groups across three AZs, plus layered admission control: token buckets, burst capacity and global admission control.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING Predictable beats fast: protect every tenant from every other tenant.

Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing A log you can read from anywhere, at the speed of the disk. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede, Jun Rao (LinkedIn) NetDB workshop, Athens 2011 · LinkedIn WHAT IT GIVES YOU The distributed log. The backbone of event-driven systems THE PAPER IN ONE LINE Combine a messaging API with an append-only, partitioned log, so one system can feed both real-time and offline consumers at high throughput. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS A notebook where people only ever write at the bottom of the page. Each reader keeps their own bookmark and reads at their own pace. Nobody erases lines, and a reader who lost their place can simply go back to an earlier page. Kafka is that notebook, spread over many machines. T HE PRO B L E M LinkedIn produced a flood of log data: page views, searches, ad impressions and operational metrics, roughly a billion messages a day. Enterprise messaging systems (ActiveMQ, RabbitMQ) focus on rich delivery guarantees, not raw throughput. Log aggregators of the time were built for offline loading into Hadoop. Kafka was designed to be both: a distributed log that real-time consumers and batch systems can read. TOPIC: page-views CONSUMER GROUPS (they pull) Group A · analytics A1 reads P0, P1 · A2 reads P2 Group B · search index B1 reads P0, P1, P2 each group tracks its own offset order exists only inside one partition → P0 → P1 → P2 partition is an append-only log; a message's address is its offset Topics are split into partitions and consumed independently by consumer groups. A topic is split into partitions, each a log stored on a broker. Producers append; consumers pull. Messages are addressed by offset (position in the log), so no random-access index is needed. A consumer group gets each message once. A partition is read by only one consumer of a group at a time, so partition count caps parallelism. Brokers are stateless about consumers. The consumer owns its offset, so it can rewind and replay. Retention is time-based (typically 7 days). H OW I T WORKS Why it is fast: boring on purpose Sequential disk Log segments of roughly 1 GB; appends and reads are sequential, which disks and the OS handle very well. OS page cache No application-level cache. Kafka relies on the OS page cache and avoids double buffering. Zero-copy sendfile copies from the file to the socket inside the kernel, skipping two copies and a system call. Batching Producers batch sends and consumers pull up to a byte limit. D e s ig n be t Simple, boring, OS-friendly I/O beats clever in-process caching. Coordination and guarantees ZooKeeper holds broker and consumer registries and the persistent offset registry. Consumers rebalance partitions among themselves. At-least-once delivery. After a consumer crash, some messages may be delivered again, so applications must de-duplicate. Ordering only within a partition. There is no global order across partitions. Each message carries a CRC to detect corruption. T he n vs . now The 2011 paper lists replication as future work; it is a core feature of Kafka today, and newer versions also offer idempotent producers and transactions. KRaft mode replaces ZooKeeper with a Raft-based quorum (see Chapter 3). Use the paper for the why, and the current docs for the how. NUM BE RS WORT H KNOW I N G Producer throughput (thousand messages per second) Batch size 1 ≈ 50k Batch size 50 ≈ 400k Batching alone gave Kafka roughly an 8× boost in the paper’s producer test. ≈ 400k messages per second produced, batch of 50 ≈ 9 B storage overhead per message (ActiveMQ: 144 B) ≈ 22k messages per second per consumer, over 4× the others ≈ 1 B messages per day at LinkedIn at the time The test compared Kafka with ActiveMQ v5.4 and RabbitMQ v2.4 on two Linux machines, with 200-byte messages. Treat the absolute numbers as 2011 hardware and the ratios as the lesson. K E Y T E RMS Topic A named stream of messages. Partition One ordered log within a topic. The unit of parallelism and ordering. Offset A message’s position in its partition. Consumer group Consumers that share the work of reading a topic. W HA T I T GI V E S UP No per-message routing or priorities, and no broker-side tracking of who has read what. Consumer-group rebalances pause consumption, and a hot partition key limits throughput. US E I T I N YOUR WORK Your key is your ordering and your parallelism. Same key → same partition → ordered. Size partitions for your maximum consumer parallelism. With Spring Kafka, commit offsets after processing and make handlers idempotent. Replaying from an offset then becomes a feature, not a risk. “Kafka is a partitioned, replicated commit log: sequential I/O, page cache and zero-copy make it fast, consumers pull and track offsets, and ordering exists only within a partition.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING The log is the product; consumers just remember where they stopped.

Scaling Memcache at Facebook How a humble cache survived billions of requests per second. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Rajesh Nishtala, Hans Fugal, Steven Grimm, et al. (Facebook) NSDI 2013 · Facebook WHAT IT GIVES YOU Cache-aside, stampede control, and cross-region invalidation THE PAPER IN ONE LINE A cache is a distributed system too: look-aside reads, delete-on-write, leases for stampedes, and invalidation streams from the database log. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS A popular dish at a canteen is kept ready at the counter (the cache). When the recipe changes, you throw away the old batch instead of trying to edit it, so no one is served a half-updated plate. And if a thousand people ask for a dish that just ran out, only one person goes to the kitchen. T HE PRO B L E M Facebook’s workload was overwhelmingly reads: pages assembled from many small pieces of data fetched from MySQL. The paper’s headline: their memcache deployment handles billions of requests per second and holds trillions of items. The authors describe growing a simple in-memory cache from one cluster, to many clusters, to many regions, and what broke at each step. Step 1: one cluster, look-aside caching R EAD 1 try the cache 2 on a miss, read MySQL 3 fill the cache WRITE 1 update MySQL 2 DELETE the cached key (never "set" it) 3 next read refills it The cache is dumb; the app and database do the work. Deleting on write keeps it simple and safe. Delete is idempotent; “set” can race and leave stale data. So after updating the database, you delete the cached key and let the next read refill it. Clients do the work. A client library (and a proxy called mcrouter) handles routing and batching, so servers stay simple. Gets use UDP to reduce overhead; sets and deletes use TCP. A sliding window limits in-flight requests to avoid network congestion on fan-in (“incast”). Two problems solved by leases A lease token fixes stampedes and stale sets at the same time. Stale set A slow client writes an old value after a newer delete. A set with an invalidated token is rejected. Thundering herd A hot key is deleted and thousands of readers rush to the database. Only one reader gets the lease; the others are told to wait briefly. The paper rate-limits lease tokens per key (by default one every 10 seconds). Surviving failures: pools and gutters Pools Different workloads get separate memcache pools, so a churny low-value workload cannot evict valuable data. Gutter A small pool of idle machines takes over for failed servers. Gutter entries expire quickly instead of being invalidated, protecting the database during outages. Steps 2 and 3: many clusters, many regions Invalidation pipeline: a daemon (McSqueal) reads the MySQL commit log and broadcasts the deletes to every cache cluster. Applications need not remember every place to invalidate. Regional pools: rarely accessed, bulky data is cached once per region instead of once per cluster, to save memory. Cold cluster warm-up: a new empty cluster can fetch from a warm one instead of hitting the database. Across regions: one region holds the master databases; others replicate from it. After a write in a replica region, a remote marker tells reads to go to the master region until replication catches up. That trades latency for avoiding a stale read of your own write. Large-scale Cluster Management at Google with Borg The cluster brain that inspired Kubernetes. AUTHORS VENUE YEAR Abhishek Verma, Luis Pedrosa, Madhukar Korupolu, David Oppenheimer, Eric Tune, John Wilkes EuroSys 2015 · Google WHAT IT GIVES YOU Scheduling, priorities, and a decade of operations lessons THE PAPER IN ONE LINE One replicated brain and a small agent per machine can run an entire company’s workloads at high utilization, if scheduling, quota and priorities are done right. I N E V E RY DA Y T E RMS A hotel manager assigning guests to rooms. VIP bookings are placed first. Cheaper guests fill what is left, and can be moved if a VIP arrives. Each floor has a supervisor reporting back to the manager. Borg is that hotel, with machines as rooms. T HE PRO B L E M Google runs hundreds of thousands of jobs from many thousands of applications across clusters of up to tens of thousands of machines. Borg is the internal cluster manager that decides where each piece of work runs, restarts it when machines fail, and keeps the hardware busy. This is the paper that explains the ancestry of Kubernetes. BORGMASTER · 5 replicas, Paxos-elected leader machine 1 · Borglet machine 2 · Borglet machine 3 · Borglet task task task task task task task task task containers containers containers A logically centralized, replicated brain and a small agent on every machine. A cell is a set of machines managed as one unit (the median is about 10,000 machines). Users submit jobs, each made of one or more tasks that run in containers. The spec is declarative: “run 200 of these, 2 GB each, priority X”. The Borgmaster is replicated five times with a Paxos-elected leader. On every machine, a Borglet starts and stops tasks and reports health. Allocs reserve resources on a machine into which several tasks can be placed (the ancestor of the Kubernetes pod). Naming and monitoring are built in: tasks get stable names, and jobs have realtime monitoring. Scheduling: two steps Highest-priority (production) work is placed first; batch work soaks up leftover capacity. Feasibility finds machines that meet the task’s constraints and have enough resources (counting resources that could be freed by preempting lower-priority tasks). Scoring then picks among them, balancing goals such as spreading across failure domains, packing machines tightly, and minimizing disruption. How Borg keeps utilization high Admission control and quota: users get a quota per priority; jobs above quota are rejected at submission. Priorities and preemption: production services outrank batch; batch soaks up leftover capacity and is preempted when needed. Over-commitment and reclamation: tasks request generous limits, but the system estimates actual use and lends the unused remainder to low-priority work. Prod and batch share machines, with process-level performance isolation. Built for availability Failed tasks are rescheduled automatically. The scheduler avoids placing a job’s tasks together where one failure would take them all. Running tasks continue even if the Borgmaster or a Borglet is briefly down. Lessons the authors learned What they would change Jobs as the only grouping mechanism is restrictive (Kubernetes uses labels). One IP per machine complicates things (Kubernetes gives each pod its own IP). The system favoured power users over casual ones. What held up Allocs are useful. Cluster management is more than task management. Introspection is vital. The master is the kernel of a distributed system, so keep it a clean API. W HA T I T GI V E S UP Borg is a centrally scheduled, tightly co-designed system, with complexity in the scheduler and in resource estimation. Over-commitment means an occasional unlucky co-location, which is why tasks must handle preemption. US E I T I N YOUR WORK In your Spring Boot deployments, requests are reservations and limits are ceilings: set both honestly. Use readiness probes so traffic only reaches healthy pods, PodDisruptionBudgets to keep replicas alive during maintenance, and expect every task to be killed and restarted at any time. It schedules by feasibility then scoring, uses priorities, quota and resource reclamation for high utilization, and Kubernetes carries its core ideas.” IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING Reserve honestly, prioritise clearly, and assume every task will be restarted.
